name: Social media detox

card.summary: Taking a deliberate break from social platforms to curb comparison; trials show small and mixed effects on well-being.
card.note: Effects in meta-analyses are small and inconsistent; some people report increased fear of missing out.

quick.overview:
A social media detox is a deliberate period of reduced or stopped use of platforms. In looksmaxxing-adjacent discussion it is raised as a way to reduce appearance comparison.

Meta-analyses of randomised trials report small and sometimes inconsistent effects on well-being.
quick.mechanism: People limit or abstain from apps for days to weeks, sometimes using blocking tools. Researchers measure well-being, depression, body image and problematic use before and after.[1][2]
quick.risks: No physical risks. Wikipedia notes detoxes can increase fear of missing out and social pressure, and that evidence is mixed.[3]

lead: A social media detox, a form of digital detox, is a deliberate break from social media or other devices, ranging from usage limits to complete abstinence for a set period.[3]

Research is mixed. Wikipedia summarises a 2024 meta-analysis that found reduced depression but no significant effect on well-being, life satisfaction or stress, and other meta-analyses reporting small improvements in well-being.[3] A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined detox and well-being,[2] and a 2025 study in Body Image compared detox strategies for body image and well-being.[4]
Sources note that exposure to idealised images is linked with body dissatisfaction in experiments,[5] which is why detoxes appear in appearance-related self-improvement discussion.

paras: Approaches include full abstinence, time limits and app blockers.[3] A survey study examined users' perceptions of detox apps in relation to personality traits.[6]

Meta-analytic findings are small and inconsistent across reviews.[3][1][2] Wikipedia notes critics argue social media provides social capital and that moderation may be preferable to abstinence.[3] A study of relapse predictors examined why people return to use.[7]

A systematic review and meta-analysis examined digital detox interventions and mental health outcomes.[1] A 2025 meta-analysis of randomised trials examined detox and well-being.[2] An exploratory two-week detox study in young adults measured problematic smartphone and social media use and related health outcomes.[8] A 2025 trial reported on in Body Image compared detox approaches for body image and well-being.[4] Experimental reviews on idealised social media images and body dissatisfaction are summarised by Wikipedia.[5]
